record.paper_title: Classification of Finite Groups: Recent Developements and Open Problems
record.context_brief: orders with at most five prime factors
record.original_question: Determine, up to isomorphism, the finite groups whose order has at most five prime factors, extending the existing complete classification for the case of at most four prime factors. An especially important part of the problem is whether this extension can be achieved by symbolic computation rather than only by case distinctions and hand calculations, so that the resulting method is more efficient.

evidence.quote: Problem 5 Determine the groups whose order factorizes into at most 5 primes. This would extend the work by Dietrich et al. [ 15] which has been achieved by case distinctions and hand calculations. It would be particularly interesting if the posed problem could be solved in a different way using symbolic computations, as this would make the solution more efﬁcient.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer n, let Ω(n) denote the number of prime factors of n counted with multiplicity, so that if n = p_1^{a_1} p_2^{a_2} ... p_k^{a_k} is the prime factorization, then Ω(n) = a_1 + a_2 + ... + a_k. A complete classification (up to isomorphism) is known for all finite groups whose order n satisfies Ω(n) ≤ 4; these correspond to the orders of the forms p^4, p^3 q, p^2 q r, p^2 q^2, and p q r s (with p, q, r, s distinct primes), and was obtained through case distinctions and hand calculations.

The problem is the following:

(a) Provide a complete classification, up to isomorphism, of all finite groups whose order n satisfies Ω(n) ≤ 5. Equivalently, classify the finite groups whose order has one of the forms p^5, p^4 q, p^3 q^2, p^3 q r, p^2 q^2 r, p^2 q r s, or p q r s t, where p, q, r, s, t are distinct primes.

(b) Determine whether this classification can be carried out via a symbolic-computation method (yielding an algorithm that, for any allowed factorization type, produces a list of isomorphism class representatives) rather than by ad hoc case distinctions, in such a way that the resulting procedure is more efficient than direct hand analysis.
artifact.status_search_result: The classification of finite groups whose order has at most 4 prime factors (counted with multiplicity) is known (work by Dietrich and collaborators). No source found indicating that the analogous classification for at most 5 prime factors has been completed in general; it remains posed as an open problem, including the question of an efficient symbolic-computation approach.

status_evidence.title: Classification of Finite Groups: Recent Developments and Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: Lists open problems including determining groups whose order factorizes into at most 5 primes, extending Dietrich et al.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is posed as open, asking for an extension from four to five prime factors, preferably via symbolic computation.

status_evidence.title: Classification of finite simple groups whose order has at most five prime factors counting multiplicities
status_evidence.snippet: Only the simple case (PSL(2,5), PSL(2,7), PSL(2,11), PSL(2,13)) is classified for at most five prime factors; the general finite group case is not.
status_evidence.claim: Only the simple-group sub-case is settled; general classification for Ω(n) ≤ 5 has not been found in the literature.
